notes.h: Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to the drug
notes.body:
Pharmacokinetics (PK) describes how drug concentration changes over time through absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). It explains why the same regimen gives different plasma levels in different patients.

Absorption and bioavailability
- Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. Intravenous drugs have F = 1; for an oral drug, F = AUC(oral) ÷ AUC(IV) when equal doses are compared.
- First-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver lowers F. Glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually partly to avoid it.
- Small, lipid-soluble, un-ionised molecules cross membranes most easily (pH-partition hypothesis).

Distribution
- Volume of distribution (Vd) = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration. It is an apparent volume: heavily tissue-bound drugs such as amiodarone and digoxin have a Vd far larger than total body water.
- Acidic drugs (warfarin, phenytoin) bind mainly to albumin; basic drugs bind α1-acid glycoprotein. Only unbound drug is active and available for clearance.

Metabolism
- Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) are mostly carried out by cytochrome P450 enzymes, especially CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19.
- Phase II reactions conjugate the drug (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) to make it more water-soluble. Slow acetylators are more prone to isoniazid neuropathy and hydralazine-induced lupus.
- Prodrugs need activation: codeine (to morphine via CYP2D6), clopidogrel, enalapril and azathioprine.

Excretion
- The kidney handles drugs by glomerular filtration of unbound drug, active tubular secretion and passive reabsorption. Probenecid blocks tubular secretion of penicillins.

Key relationships
- Clearance (CL) = rate of elimination ÷ plasma concentration.
- t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL.
- First-order kinetics: a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time. Zero-order (saturable) kinetics: a constant amount is removed, so a small increase in intake can cause a disproportionate rise in level (phenytoin, ethanol, salicylate in overdose).
- Steady state is reached after about 4–5 half-lives whatever the dosing rate. A loading dose (Vd × target concentration) reaches the target sooner.

Worked example
A drug has Vd 70 L and CL 7 L/h. t½ = 0.693 × 70 ÷ 7 ≈ 6.9 h, so steady state takes roughly 28–35 h. After stopping, three half-lives (about 21 h) leave 12.5% of the steady-state concentration.

Exam pitfalls
- Half-life sets the time to steady state, not the steady-state level; the level depends on dosing rate and clearance.
- A large Vd means the drug is mostly outside the plasma, not that it is concentrated in it.
- Enzyme inducers take one to two weeks to reach full effect because new enzyme must be synthesised; inhibitors act within days.

notes.h: Pharmacodynamics: what the drug does to the body
notes.body:
Pharmacodynamics (PD) describes how a drug produces its effect: which target it binds, what happens next, and how response varies with concentration.

Drug targets
- Receptors, enzymes (ACE, cyclo-oxygenase), transporters (the serotonin transporter, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) and ion channels (voltage-gated Na⁺ channels blocked by lidocaine).
- Four receptor superfamilies, from fastest to slowest:
- Ligand-gated ion channels (milliseconds): nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, 5-HT3, NMDA.
- G protein-coupled receptors (seconds): Gs raises cAMP (β-adrenoceptors); Gi lowers cAMP (α2, M2, μ-opioid); Gq activates phospholipase C to give IP3, DAG and intracellular Ca²⁺ (α1, M3, H1).
- Kinase-linked receptors (minutes to hours): the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase; cytokine receptors acting through JAK–STAT.
- Nuclear receptors (hours): corticosteroids, thyroid hormone, PPAR-γ.

Key terms
- Affinity is how tightly a drug binds (dissociation constant KD); efficacy is its ability to activate the receptor once bound.
- Potency is the concentration giving 50% of maximal effect (EC50); Emax is the maximum response. A more potent drug is not necessarily more effective.
- A partial agonist has submaximal efficacy and can antagonise a full agonist: buprenorphine at μ-opioid receptors, varenicline at nicotinic receptors.
- An inverse agonist reduces constitutive receptor activity; many H1 antihistamines behave this way.

Antagonism
- Reversible competitive antagonists cause a parallel rightward shift of the log concentration–response curve with unchanged Emax (surmountable). Schild analysis: dose ratio − 1 = [B] ÷ KB.
- Irreversible or non-competitive antagonists depress Emax: phenoxybenzamine at α-adrenoceptors. Aspirin and omeprazole irreversibly inhibit enzymes, so their effect lasts until new protein is made.
- Spare receptors mean a maximal response can occur at low occupancy, so an irreversible antagonist may initially shift the curve before depressing Emax.

Therapeutic index and adaptation
- Therapeutic index = TD50 ÷ ED50. Narrow-index drugs include digoxin, lithium, warfarin, aminoglycosides, phenytoin and theophylline.
- Tachyphylaxis is rapid loss of response (nitrate tolerance); desensitisation of β2-receptors involves GRK phosphorylation and β-arrestin binding; long-term antagonism can up-regulate receptors, causing rebound on withdrawal (abrupt β-blocker cessation).

Worked example
By the Hill–Langmuir equation, fractional occupancy p = [A] ÷ ([A] + KD). At [A] = KD, p = 0.5; at [A] = 4KD, p = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (80%).

Exam pitfalls
- Do not confuse potency with efficacy.
- A competitive antagonist does not lower Emax; a partial agonist can precipitate withdrawal in someone dependent on a full agonist.

The autonomic nervous system has two efferent limbs, and most autonomic drugs mimic or block their transmitters.

Anatomy and transmitters
- All preganglionic fibres release acetylcholine (ACh) onto nicotinic (NN) receptors in ganglia. The adrenal medulla behaves like a ganglion and releases mainly adrenaline.
- Parasympathetic postganglionic fibres release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. Sympathetic postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline onto adrenoceptors, except at sweat glands, which are cholinergic muscarinic.
- Skeletal muscle has NM nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction (somatic, not autonomic).

Receptors
- M1: CNS, gastric secretion. M2 (Gi): heart, slowing rate and AV conduction. M3 (Gq): smooth muscle contraction, glandular secretion, endothelial NO release.
- α1 (Gq): vasoconstriction, prostate and bladder-neck contraction, mydriasis. α2 (Gi): presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release.
- β1 (Gs): heart rate and contractility, renin release. β2 (Gs): bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis. β3: detrusor relaxation and lipolysis.

Key drugs
- Muscarinic antagonists: atropine (bradycardia), ipratropium and tiotropium (bronchodilation), oxybutynin (overactive bladder), hyoscine (secretions, motion sickness). Toxicity: dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, mydriasis, hyperthermia, confusion.
- Anticholinesterases: pyridostigmine (myasthenia gravis), neostigmine (reversing non-depolarising blockade, given with glycopyrronium to block muscarinic effects), donepezil (dementia). Organophosphate poisoning irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase: treat with atropine plus an oxime such as pralidoxime.
- Adrenoceptor agonists: salbutamol (β2), dobutamine (mainly β1), noradrenaline (mainly α1 and β1), adrenaline (α and β; first-line intramuscular drug in anaphylaxis), clonidine (central α2), mirabegron (β3).
- Adrenoceptor antagonists: doxazosin (α1), tamsulosin (α1A, prostate), propranolol (non-selective β), bisoprolol and atenolol (β1-selective), labetalol and carvedilol (α and β).
- Neuromuscular blockers: suxamethonium (depolarising; risks hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia, prolonged apnoea with pseudocholinesterase deficiency); rocuronium (non-depolarising competitive antagonist, reversed by sugammadex encapsulation).

Applied illustration
A patient with phaeochromocytoma must receive α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) before any β-blocker. β-blockade alone removes β2-mediated vasodilation and leaves α1 vasoconstriction unopposed, risking a hypertensive crisis.

Exam pitfalls
- β-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm in asthma; β1-selectivity is relative, not absolute.
- Combining a β-blocker with verapamil risks heart block and asystole.
- Organophosphate poisoning causes both muscarinic (secretions, bradycardia, miosis) and nicotinic (fasciculation, weakness) features; atropine treats only the muscarinic ones.

Pain management uses drugs with different mechanisms, chosen by pain type. The WHO analgesic ladder (1986) was designed for cancer pain and should not be applied uncritically to chronic non-cancer pain.

Paracetamol
- Mechanism not fully understood; likely central COX inhibition and serotonergic pathways. Analgesic and antipyretic but negligible anti-inflammatory effect.
- In overdose, saturated conjugation diverts metabolism via CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione. Since 2012 the UK uses a single treatment line on the nomogram; staggered or uncertain-time ingestions are treated without relying on it.

NSAIDs
- Inhibit cyclo-oxygenase. COX-1 is constitutive (gastric mucosal protection, platelet thromboxane A2, renal perfusion); COX-2 is induced in inflammation but also constitutive in kidney and endothelium.
- Adverse effects: peptic ulceration and bleeding, AKI (loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation), fluid retention and worsening heart failure, raised thrombotic risk, and bronchospasm in NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease.
- Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, etoricoxib) cause less GI injury but reduce endothelial prostacyclin without blocking platelet thromboxane, increasing thrombotic risk. Co-prescribe a PPI when GI risk is high.
- Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1; avoid in under-16s (Reye's syndrome).

Opioids
- μ-opioid agonists act through Gi: they reduce cAMP, open K⁺ channels and close voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, cutting neurotransmitter release in pain pathways.
- Effects: analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, nausea, constipation and pruritus. Tolerance develops to most effects but little to constipation or miosis, so prescribe a laxative.
- Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk morphine toxicity, so it is contraindicated in under-12s and in breastfeeding. Tramadol also inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake (serotonin syndrome, seizures). Morphine's active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment.
- Naloxone is a competitive antagonist with a shorter duration than many opioids, so re-sedation can occur.

Neuropathic and chronic pain
- NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain): offer amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin first line; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. Gabapentinoids have been Schedule 3 controlled drugs since 2019.
- NICE NG193 (2021, chronic primary pain): advises against starting opioids, NSAIDs, paracetamol or gabapentinoids; exercise, psychological therapy and an antidepressant may be offered.

Corticosteroids
- Bind cytosolic glucocorticoid receptors and alter gene transcription, suppressing COX-2, cytokines and phospholipase A2 activity. Long-term risks: adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, infection, myopathy and mood change. Patients need a steroid emergency card and sick-day advice.

Exam pitfalls
- Paracetamol is not anti-inflammatory; COX-2 selectivity reduces GI but not renal or cardiovascular risk.
- Do not treat opioid-induced constipation as something tolerance will fix.

These are among the most frequently prescribed drug groups, so examiners expect mechanisms, key adverse effects and guideline sequencing.

Antihypertensives
- ACE inhibitors (ramipril) block angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown: dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalaemia, AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis; contraindicated in pregnancy. ARBs (losartan) block AT1 receptors with less cough.
- Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) dilate arterioles and cause ankle oedema and flushing; rate-limiting verapamil and diltiazem slow AV conduction and should be avoided in HFrEF.
- Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide) inhibit the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule: hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia.
- NICE NG136: step 1 is an ACE inhibitor or ARB for people under 55 or with type 2 diabetes, and a CCB for those 55 or over or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin without diabetes. Step 2 adds the other class or a thiazide-like diuretic; step 3 uses all three; step 4 considers spironolactone if potassium is not raised, otherwise an α- or β-blocker.

Lipids
- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, up-regulating hepatic LDL receptors. Myopathy risk rises with CYP3A4 inhibitors (simvastatin with clarithromycin is contraindicated). NICE NG238 (2023) uses QRISK3 to guide primary prevention. Ezetimibe blocks intestinal NPC1L1; PCSK9 inhibitors and inclisiran raise LDL-receptor recycling.

Antithrombotics
- Aspirin blocks platelet thromboxane A2; clopidogrel (prodrug via CYP2C19), prasugrel and ticagrelor block P2Y12.
- Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S); monitored by INR.
- DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban inhibit factor Xa; dabigatran inhibits thrombin and is reversed by idarucizumab.
- Heparin potentiates antithrombin; LMWH acts mainly on factor Xa.

Heart failure (HFrEF)
- Prognostic therapy: ACE inhibitor (or sacubitril–valsartan), heart-failure β-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor. Loop diuretics (furosemide, blocking NKCC2) relieve congestion but do not improve survival.
- Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and enhances vagal tone; toxicity is promoted by hypokalaemia.

Respiratory
- β2 agonists (salbutamol short-acting; formoterol and salmeterol long-acting) relax airway smooth muscle; muscarinic antagonists (tiotropium) block M3. Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation.
- Asthma, NICE/BTS/SIGN NG245 (2024): for people aged 12 and over, as-needed ICS–formoterol (AIR) for new diagnoses, progressing to maintenance and reliever therapy (MART). SABA alone is no longer recommended.
- COPD, NICE NG115: SABA or SAMA first, then LABA + LAMA, or LABA + ICS if asthmatic features, then triple therapy.
- Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and CYP1A2 metabolism; smoking induces it.

Exam pitfalls
- Never combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB routinely.
- Salmeterol and other LABAs must not be used in asthma without an ICS.

CNS pharmacology is examined through mechanism, characteristic toxicity and safety-critical interactions.

Antidepressants
- SSRIs (sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine) block the serotonin transporter. Adverse effects: GI upset, hyponatraemia (especially in older people), GI bleeding (worse with NSAIDs or anticoagulants), sexual dysfunction and, with citalopram, QT prolongation. Suicidal thinking can increase early in treatment in young people.
- SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) also block noradrenaline reuptake. Mirtazapine antagonises α2 and 5-HT2/3 receptors (weight gain, sedation).
- TCAs (amitriptyline) block amine reuptake plus muscarinic, H1 and α1 receptors; in overdose they block cardiac Na⁺ channels (broad QRS, arrhythmia, seizures), treated with sodium bicarbonate.
- MAOIs cause hypertensive crises with dietary tyramine.
- Serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, agitation) follows combinations such as an SSRI with an MAOI, tramadol, linezolid or St John's wort.

Lithium
- Narrow therapeutic index; handled renally like sodium. Dehydration, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs raise levels.
- Toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures. Long term: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hypercalcaemia.

Antipsychotics
- Block dopamine D2 receptors in mesolimbic pathways. First-generation drugs (haloperidol) commonly cause extrapyramidal effects and hyperprolactinaemia; second-generation drugs (olanzapine) cause more weight gain and metabolic disturbance.
- Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires registration and mandatory blood monitoring for agranulocytosis; it also causes severe constipation and myocarditis. Stopping smoking raises clozapine levels because tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2.
- Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and raised CK.

Antiepileptics
- Na⁺ channel blockers: carbamazepine (enzyme inducer, hyponatraemia; HLA-B*15:02 predicts Stevens–Johnson syndrome), phenytoin (zero-order kinetics, gum hypertrophy, cerebellar signs), lamotrigine (rash; levels doubled by valproate). Levetiracetam binds SV2A. Ethosuximide blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels in absence seizures.
- Valproate is highly teratogenic. MHRA (2024): it must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that no other treatment is effective or tolerated, or that there are compelling reasons the reproductive risks do not apply; this applies to males and females, and those who can become pregnant must follow the Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

Anxiolytics and hypnotics
- Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, increasing the frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening. Risks: dependence, falls, respiratory depression with opioids. Flumazenil reverses them but can provoke seizures.

Parkinson's and dementia
- Levodopa is combined with a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide). Dopamine agonists can cause impulse-control disorders. Avoid metoclopramide and haloperidol; domperidone acts peripherally.
- Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) and the NMDA antagonist memantine are used in Alzheimer's disease.

Exam pitfalls
- Carbamazepine can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.
- Do not confuse serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, clonus) with NMS (slower onset, lead-pipe rigidity).

An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response to a medicine at normal use. ADRs cause a substantial share of hospital admissions, especially in older people with polypharmacy.

Classification
- Rawlins–Thompson: Type A (augmented, dose-related, predictable from pharmacology, e.g. bleeding with warfarin) and Type B (bizarre, not dose-related, e.g. anaphylaxis to penicillin). Later additions: C (chronic, e.g. steroid osteoporosis), D (delayed, e.g. teratogenicity), E (end of use, e.g. benzodiazepine withdrawal) and F (failure of therapy, e.g. contraceptive failure with enzyme inducers).
- DoTS (Aronson and Ferner, 2003) describes ADRs by dose relatedness, timing and patient susceptibility.
- Immunological reactions follow Gell and Coombs types I–IV. Severe cutaneous reactions include Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN (allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfonamides) and DRESS.

Pharmacokinetic interactions
- Absorption: calcium, iron and antacids chelate tetracyclines, quinolones and levothyroxine.
- Metabolism: inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, St John's wort, chronic alcohol) lower levels of warfarin, combined hormonal contraceptives and ciclosporin. Inhibitors (clarithromycin, azole antifungals, grapefruit juice, ritonavir, amiodarone) raise levels of statins, warfarin and others.
- Excretion: thiazides, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance; NSAIDs and probenecid reduce methotrexate clearance.
- Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, so azathioprine and mercaptopurine accumulate, causing marrow suppression.

Pharmacodynamic interactions
- Additive QT prolongation: macrolides, quinolones, antipsychotics, citalopram, methadone, ondansetron, amiodarone.
- Hyperkalaemia: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus spironolactone or trimethoprim.
- "Triple whammy" AKI: ACE inhibitor or ARB, diuretic and NSAID together.
- Bleeding: anticoagulant plus NSAID or SSRI.
- CNS and respiratory depression: opioid plus benzodiazepine or gabapentinoid.
- Serotonin syndrome: combinations of serotonergic drugs.

Pharmacovigilance
- The thalidomide disaster led to the Committee on Safety of Drugs (1963) and the Medicines Act 1968. The Yellow Card scheme (MHRA) collects suspected ADR reports from professionals and the public; report all suspected reactions to black-triangle (▼) medicines and serious reactions to any medicine.

Worked example
A woman stable on warfarin is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and alters gut flora, so her INR may rise sharply and cause bleeding. Choose a non-interacting antibiotic where appropriate, or check the INR within a few days and adjust.

Exam pitfalls
- Type B reactions are not "rare Type A" reactions; they are unrelated to the known pharmacology.
- Protein-binding displacement rarely causes lasting clinical interactions because free drug is cleared faster.
- Penicillin "allergy" labels are often wrong; distinguish intolerance from true hypersensitivity.

Safe prescribing combines legal requirements, good clinical reasoning and attention to the individual patient. The GMC's Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021) sets professional standards, and UK final-year students sit the Prescribing Safety Assessment.

Before prescribing
- Take a full drug history: prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines, adherence, allergies with the nature of the reaction, alcohol and recreational drugs. Medicines reconciliation at admission and discharge prevents omissions and duplications.
- Consider indication, contraindications, interactions and patient factors: age, weight, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy and breastfeeding.
- Share decisions with patients (NICE NG197, 2021): discuss benefits, risks and alternatives in understandable terms.

Writing the prescription
- Approved (generic) names except where brand matters (e.g. some modified-release products, ciclosporin, certain antiepileptics); clear route, frequency, start date, indication and review date; legible signature.
- Avoid abbreviations: write "units" and "micrograms" in full and never use a trailing zero.
- Controlled drugs (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001): Schedule 2 and 3 prescriptions need form, strength and the total quantity in words and figures, and are valid for 28 days.

Patient groups
- Renal impairment: reduce or avoid renally cleared drugs (gentamicin, DOACs, metformin, lithium, morphine). For some drugs, estimate creatinine clearance with Cockcroft–Gault rather than eGFR.
- Hepatic impairment: beware sedatives, opioids (risk of encephalopathy) and drugs causing fluid retention or bleeding.
- Pregnancy: avoid known teratogens such as valproate, isotretinoin, warfarin, methotrexate and ACE inhibitors (particularly later in pregnancy).
- Older people: polypharmacy and falls risk. Tools such as STOPP/START help identify inappropriate drugs; anticholinergic burden worsens cognition. Deprescribing is an active, planned intervention (NICE NG5, medicines optimisation).

High-risk medicines
- Anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, methotrexate (taken once weekly; daily-dosing errors have been fatal), intravenous potassium, aminoglycosides and lithium. Therapeutic drug monitoring guides gentamicin, vancomycin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin and tacrolimus.

Worked example
An 80-year-old woman weighing 60 kg has serum creatinine 100 µmol/L. Cockcroft–Gault: CrCl = (140 − 80) × 60 × 1.04 ÷ 100 = 3744 ÷ 100 ≈ 37 mL/min. Her eGFR may look reassuring, but this estimate shows moderately reduced clearance, which matters when choosing or adjusting a DOAC.

Exam pitfalls
- eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m² body surface area; at extremes of weight, absolute clearance may differ markedly.
- An allergy box saying "penicillin" without the reaction is incomplete.
- Report suspected ADRs via the Yellow Card scheme; it does not require certainty of causation.

cards.f: Define bioavailability (F).
cards.b: The fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. It is 1 for IV drugs and is found for oral drugs as AUC(oral) ÷ AUC(IV) with equal doses.

cards.f: Define volume of distribution (Vd).
cards.b: The apparent volume into which a drug would have to distribute to give the observed plasma concentration: amount in body ÷ plasma concentration. It is not a real anatomical space.

cards.f: Give the formula linking half-life, Vd and clearance.
cards.b: t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL. A larger Vd or a smaller clearance both prolong the half-life.

cards.f: How long does it take to reach steady state on regular dosing?
cards.b: About 4–5 half-lives, regardless of the dosing rate. A loading dose reaches the target concentration sooner.

cards.f: First-order vs zero-order elimination?
cards.b: First-order: a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time, so the rate is proportional to concentration. Zero-order: elimination enzymes are saturated, so a constant amount is removed per unit time.

cards.f: Name three drugs that show zero-order (saturable) kinetics clinically.
cards.b: Phenytoin (within the therapeutic range), ethanol, and salicylate in overdose. Small increases in intake can cause disproportionate rises in plasma level.

cards.f: What is first-pass metabolism? Give an example of a route chosen to avoid it.
cards.b: Metabolism of an oral drug in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation, which lowers bioavailability. Glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually partly to bypass it.

cards.f: Distinguish phase I and phase II metabolism.
cards.b: Phase I adds or exposes a functional group by oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis, mostly via CYP450 enzymes. Phase II conjugates the drug (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) to make it more water-soluble for excretion.

cards.f: Name four prodrugs and their activation step.
cards.b: Codeine to morphine (CYP2D6); clopidogrel to its active thiol metabolite (largely CYP2C19); enalapril to enalaprilat (hepatic esterases); azathioprine to mercaptopurine.

cards.f: Why do enzyme inducers take longer to act than enzyme inhibitors?
cards.b: Induction requires new enzyme synthesis, so full effect takes one to two weeks and also wears off slowly. Inhibition acts on existing enzyme, so it appears within days as the inhibitor reaches steady state.

cards.f: How does urinary alkalinisation help in salicylate poisoning?
cards.b: Salicylate is a weak acid. Raising urine pH increases its ionised fraction in the tubule, which cannot be passively reabsorbed (ion trapping), so excretion rises.

cards.f: Why is phenytoin level interpretation difficult in hypoalbuminaemia?
cards.b: Phenytoin is highly albumin-bound and assays usually measure total drug. With low albumin the free (active) fraction is higher, so a 'normal' total level may hide toxicity.

cards.f: Distinguish affinity and efficacy.
cards.b: Affinity is how strongly a drug binds its receptor (reflected by KD). Efficacy is its ability, once bound, to activate the receptor and produce a response.

cards.f: Distinguish potency and efficacy.
cards.b: Potency is the concentration needed for a given effect (EC50); efficacy is the maximum effect achievable (Emax). A more potent drug is not necessarily more effective.

cards.f: What is a partial agonist? Give two examples.
cards.b: An agonist with submaximal efficacy that cannot produce a full response even at full occupancy, and can antagonise a full agonist. Examples: buprenorphine (μ-opioid) and varenicline (nicotinic receptors).

cards.f: Effect of a reversible competitive antagonist on the log concentration–response curve?
cards.b: A parallel rightward shift with unchanged maximum response; the antagonism is surmountable by more agonist.

cards.f: Effect of an irreversible antagonist on the concentration–response curve?
cards.b: It reduces the maximum response (Emax); with spare receptors there may first be a rightward shift before Emax falls. Example: phenoxybenzamine at α-adrenoceptors.

cards.f: Which G protein does each couple to: β-adrenoceptor, α2, M3?
cards.b: β-adrenoceptors couple to Gs (raises cAMP); α2 to Gi (lowers cAMP); M3 to Gq (phospholipase C, IP3, DAG, raised intracellular Ca²⁺).

cards.f: Name the four receptor superfamilies in order of response speed.
cards.b: Ligand-gated ion channels (milliseconds), G protein-coupled receptors (seconds), kinase-linked receptors (minutes–hours), nuclear receptors (hours).

cards.f: Define therapeutic index and name four narrow-index drugs.
cards.b: Therapeutic index = TD50 ÷ ED50, the ratio of toxic to effective median concentrations or doses. Narrow examples: digoxin, lithium, warfarin, gentamicin (also phenytoin, theophylline).

cards.f: What is an inverse agonist?
cards.b: A drug that binds a receptor with constitutive activity and reduces that baseline activity, producing an effect opposite to an agonist. Many H1 antihistamines act this way.

cards.f: State the Schild equation.
cards.b: Dose ratio − 1 = [B] ÷ KB, where [B] is antagonist concentration and KB its dissociation constant. A Schild plot slope of 1 is consistent with simple competitive antagonism.

cards.f: Calculate fractional occupancy when agonist concentration equals 9 × KD.
cards.b: p = [A] ÷ ([A] + KD) = 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9, so 90% of receptors are occupied.

cards.f: Why can buprenorphine precipitate withdrawal in someone dependent on heroin?
cards.b: Buprenorphine binds μ-receptors with high affinity but lower efficacy, displacing the full agonist. Net receptor activation falls, causing withdrawal.

cards.f: What is tachyphylaxis? Give an example.
cards.b: Rapid loss of response to repeated drug exposure, developing over minutes to hours. Continuous nitrate exposure produces tolerance, prevented by a nitrate-free period.

cards.f: Which neurotransmitter and receptor operate at all autonomic ganglia?
cards.b: Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic (NN) receptors, in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.

cards.f: Which sympathetic target organ uses acetylcholine at the postganglionic synapse?
cards.b: Eccrine sweat glands, which have muscarinic receptors despite sympathetic innervation.

cards.f: List the clinical features of anticholinergic toxicity.
cards.b: Dry hot flushed skin, tachycardia, dilated pupils and blurred vision, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds, hyperthermia, agitation and confusion.

cards.f: Treatment of organophosphate poisoning?
cards.b: Decontamination, airway support, atropine to reverse muscarinic effects (dry the secretions) and an oxime such as pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before 'ageing'. Benzodiazepines for seizures.

cards.f: Why is adrenaline the first-line drug in anaphylaxis?
cards.b: α1 vasoconstriction reverses hypotension and mucosal oedema; β1 increases cardiac output; β2 causes bronchodilation and reduces mast cell mediator release. It is given intramuscularly.

cards.f: Why must α-blockade precede β-blockade in phaeochromocytoma?
cards.b: β-blockade alone removes β2-mediated vasodilation, leaving catecholamine-driven α1 vasoconstriction unopposed and risking a hypertensive crisis.

cards.f: Why is neostigmine given with glycopyrronium when reversing neuromuscular blockade?
cards.b: Neostigmine raises ACh at muscarinic as well as nicotinic synapses, causing bradycardia, secretions and bronchospasm. Glycopyrronium blocks the muscarinic effects without crossing the blood–brain barrier.

cards.f: How does sugammadex work?
cards.b: It is a modified cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium in plasma, removing it from the neuromuscular junction. It does not act on acetylcholinesterase.

cards.f: Name three risks of suxamethonium.
cards.b: Hyperkalaemia (especially after burns, crush injury or denervation), malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients, and prolonged apnoea with plasma cholinesterase deficiency. It also causes fasciculations and myalgia.

cards.f: Which adrenoceptor does mirabegron target, and for what?
cards.b: β3-adrenoceptors in the detrusor, causing relaxation; used for overactive bladder as an alternative to antimuscarinics, with less anticholinergic burden.

cards.f: Contrast tamsulosin and doxazosin.
cards.b: Both block α1-adrenoceptors. Tamsulosin is relatively selective for α1A in the prostate, so it is used for BPH symptoms with less hypotension; doxazosin is non-selective α1 and also lowers blood pressure.

cards.f: Why is combining a β-blocker with verapamil dangerous?
cards.b: Both depress SA and AV nodal conduction and contractility, risking severe bradycardia, heart block, hypotension and asystole.

cards.f: What is the toxic metabolite in paracetamol overdose and how is it detoxified?
cards.b: NAPQI, produced via CYP2E1 when conjugation pathways saturate. It is normally neutralised by glutathione; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.

cards.f: Why do COX-2-selective NSAIDs carry increased thrombotic risk?
cards.b: They reduce endothelial prostacyclin (antiaggregatory, vasodilatory) without inhibiting platelet COX-1 thromboxane A2, tipping the balance toward thrombosis.

cards.f: How do NSAIDs cause acute kidney injury?
cards.b: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole when renal perfusion is threatened. NSAIDs remove this, reducing glomerular filtration, especially with dehydration, ACE inhibitors/ARBs or diuretics.

cards.f: Why is aspirin avoided in children under 16?
cards.b: Because of the association with Reye's syndrome, an acute encephalopathy with fatty liver, usually after a viral illness.

cards.f: Cellular mechanism of μ-opioid agonists?
cards.b: Gi coupling reduces cAMP, opens K⁺ channels (hyperpolarisation) and closes presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, reducing neurotransmitter release in nociceptive pathways.

cards.f: To which opioid effects does little tolerance develop?
cards.b: Constipation and miosis. Laxatives should be co-prescribed with regular opioids.

cards.f: Why is codeine contraindicated in children under 12 and in breastfeeding?
cards.b: Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers can form dangerous amounts of morphine, causing respiratory depression in children or breastfed infants.

cards.f: Why does a patient given naloxone need continued observation?
cards.b: Naloxone's duration of action is shorter than that of many opioids, so respiratory depression can return once it wears off; repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

cards.f: Name the first-line options for neuropathic pain in NICE CG173.
cards.b: A choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (switching if not effective or tolerated). Carbamazepine is first line for trigeminal neuralgia.

cards.f: What two extra actions make tramadol different from other opioids?
cards.b: It inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake as well as acting as a weak μ agonist, so it can cause serotonin syndrome and lowers the seizure threshold.

cards.f: How do glucocorticoids produce anti-inflammatory effects?
cards.b: They bind cytosolic glucocorticoid receptors that move to the nucleus and alter gene transcription, reducing COX-2, cytokines and other inflammatory mediators and inhibiting phospholipase A2 activity.

cards.f: What does NICE NG193 (2021) advise about drugs for chronic primary pain?
cards.b: Do not start opioids, NSAIDs, paracetamol, gabapentinoids or benzodiazepines for chronic primary pain. Antidepressants may be considered alongside exercise and psychological therapies.

cards.f: Why do ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough, and what is the alternative?
cards.b: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; its accumulation in the airway causes cough. An angiotensin II receptor blocker avoids this.

cards.f: Give three adverse effects of thiazide-like diuretics.
cards.b: Hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia and hypercalcaemia; any three.

cards.f: NICE NG136 step 1 antihypertensive for a 62-year-old without diabetes?
cards.b: A calcium channel blocker, because they are aged 55 or over. (An ACE inhibitor or ARB would be first for under-55s or anyone with type 2 diabetes.)

cards.f: Mechanism of warfarin?
cards.b: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

cards.f: Which DOAC has a specific reversal agent idarucizumab?
cards.b: Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds it.

cards.f: Name the four drug classes that improve prognosis in HFrEF.
cards.b: ACE inhibitor/ARB or sacubitril–valsartan; a heart-failure β-blocker; a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

cards.f: Why does hypokalaemia increase the risk of digoxin toxicity?
cards.b: Digoxin and K⁺ compete for binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; with low K⁺, more digoxin binds, enhancing toxicity.

cards.f: Where and how do loop diuretics act?
cards.b: They inhibit the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, producing a powerful diuresis.

cards.f: What reliever approach does NG245 (2024) recommend for newly diagnosed asthma in people aged 12 and over?
cards.b: As-needed ICS–formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, AIR), rather than a SABA alone. MART is used if symptoms are more severe or control is poor.

cards.f: Why must a LABA never be used alone in asthma?
cards.b: LABA monotherapy controls symptoms while leaving airway inflammation untreated and is associated with increased risk of severe and fatal attacks; it should always be given with an ICS.

cards.f: Why should nitrates not be combined with PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil?
cards.b: Both increase cGMP-mediated vasodilation; together they can cause profound hypotension.

cards.f: How do statins lower LDL cholesterol?
cards.b: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis; falling hepatocyte cholesterol up-regulates LDL receptors, increasing LDL clearance from blood.

cards.f: Contrast clopidogrel and ticagrelor.
cards.b: Both block the platelet P2Y12 receptor. Clopidogrel is an irreversible prodrug needing CYP2C19 activation; ticagrelor acts directly and reversibly.

cards.f: List the features of serotonin syndrome.
cards.b: Neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhoea) and altered mental state, developing rapidly after a serotonergic drug change.

cards.f: Which drugs commonly raise lithium levels?
cards.b: Thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs, plus dehydration or sodium depletion.

cards.f: Long-term adverse effects of lithium?
cards.b: Hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia, and weight gain.

cards.f: Why does clozapine need mandatory blood monitoring?
cards.b: It can cause agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), so patients are registered with a monitoring service and full blood counts must be checked before supply.

cards.f: Why might a patient's clozapine level rise when they stop smoking?
cards.b: Polycyclic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2, which metabolises clozapine; stopping smoking removes the induction, so levels rise and toxicity can follow.

cards.f: Features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
cards.b: Lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and markedly raised creatine kinase, developing over days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic.

cards.f: Why is levodopa combined with carbidopa or benserazide?
cards.b: They inhibit peripheral dopa decarboxylase (they do not cross the blood–brain barrier), so more levodopa reaches the brain and peripheral side-effects such as nausea are reduced.

cards.f: Which genetic marker predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome?
cards.b: HLA-B*15:02, most common in people of Han Chinese and some other Southeast Asian ancestries; testing is advised before starting carbamazepine in these groups.

cards.f: How do benzodiazepines differ from barbiturates at the GABA-A receptor?
cards.b: Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of chloride channel opening; barbiturates increase the duration of opening and at high concentrations can open the channel directly.

cards.f: Why does sodium valproate affect lamotrigine therapy?
cards.b: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, roughly doubling lamotrigine levels and increasing the risk of serious rash, so lamotrigine titration must be slower.

cards.f: What are the 2024 MHRA restrictions on starting valproate?
cards.b: It must not be started in patients under 55 unless two specialists independently document that no other effective or tolerated treatment exists, or that there are compelling reasons the reproductive risks do not apply (this applies to males and females); those able to become pregnant must also follow the Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

cards.f: Why do tricyclic overdoses broaden the QRS, and what is the antidote approach?
cards.b: TCAs block fast cardiac Na⁺ channels, slowing conduction. Sodium bicarbonate (alkalinisation plus a sodium load) is used to narrow the QRS and reduce arrhythmia risk.

cards.f: Distinguish Type A and Type B adverse drug reactions.
cards.b: Type A (augmented) reactions are dose-related and predictable from known pharmacology. Type B (bizarre) reactions are unpredictable, not clearly dose-related, and often immunological or idiosyncratic.

cards.f: Give an example of each of Types C, D, E and F reactions.
cards.b: C: osteoporosis with long-term corticosteroids. D: teratogenesis with valproate. E: rebound/withdrawal after stopping benzodiazepines. F: contraceptive failure with an enzyme inducer.

cards.f: What does DoTS stand for?
cards.b: Dose relatedness, Timing and Susceptibility: a classification of ADRs described by Aronson and Ferner (2003).

cards.f: Name four potent CYP450 enzyme inducers.
cards.b: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin and St John's wort (also phenobarbital and chronic alcohol use).

cards.f: Name four CYP3A4 inhibitors.
cards.b: Clarithromycin/erythromycin, azole antifungals (ketoconazole, itraconazole), ritonavir and grapefruit juice.

cards.f: Why is azathioprine dangerous with allopurinol?
cards.b: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which inactivates mercaptopurine (azathioprine's metabolite). Accumulation causes severe bone marrow suppression.

cards.f: What is the 'triple whammy'?
cards.b: The combination of an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a diuretic and an NSAID, which together impair renal autoregulation and markedly increase the risk of AKI.

cards.f: Why should tetracyclines not be taken with milk or iron?
cards.b: Divalent and trivalent cations such as calcium and iron chelate tetracyclines in the gut, reducing absorption.

cards.f: Which drug classes cause QT prolongation? Name four.
cards.b: Macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, some SSRIs (citalopram), methadone, ondansetron and class III antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone; any four.

cards.f: What is the black triangle symbol (▼)?
cards.b: It marks medicines under additional monitoring by the MHRA, typically new drugs or new uses. All suspected ADRs to them should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.

cards.f: Which drugs commonly cause Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN?
cards.b: Allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides (including co-trimoxazole) and some NSAIDs.

cards.f: Why do protein-binding displacement interactions rarely matter clinically?
cards.b: Displacement raises free drug briefly, but more free drug is then cleared, so the free concentration returns towards baseline; it matters mainly for interpreting total levels.

cards.f: What should an allergy entry on a drug chart include?
cards.b: The drug or substance and the nature of the reaction (e.g. rash, anaphylaxis), so true allergy can be distinguished from intolerance.

cards.f: Additional prescription requirements for Schedule 2 and 3 controlled drugs?
cards.b: Drug form and strength, and the total quantity in both words and figures, as well as the usual details; the prescription is valid for 28 days.

cards.f: Why must 'units' and 'micrograms' be written in full?
cards.b: Abbreviations such as 'U' and 'µg' are easily misread (e.g. U as 0, µg as mg), causing tenfold or thousandfold errors.

cards.f: Why is methotrexate a high-risk medicine?
cards.b: It is taken once weekly for inflammatory disease; accidental daily dosing has caused fatal marrow suppression. It also needs blood monitoring and has important interactions (e.g. trimethoprim).

cards.f: State the Cockcroft–Gault equation in UK units.
cards.b: CrCl (mL/min) = (140 − age) × weight (kg) × F ÷ serum creatinine (µmol/L), where F is 1.23 for men and 1.04 for women.

cards.f: Why may creatinine clearance be preferred to eGFR for some drugs?
cards.b: eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m² body surface area and is less reliable at extremes of weight; Cockcroft–Gault estimates absolute clearance, which is what licensing data for many renally cleared drugs used.

cards.f: What is medicines reconciliation?
cards.b: Compiling an accurate list of a patient's current medicines from at least two sources and comparing it with prescriptions at transitions of care, resolving discrepancies.

cards.f: Name four drugs needing therapeutic drug monitoring.
cards.b: Gentamicin, vancomycin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, ciclosporin or tacrolimus; any four.

cards.f: What are STOPP/START criteria?
cards.b: Explicit screening tools for older adults: STOPP lists potentially inappropriate prescriptions, START lists potentially omitted beneficial treatments.

cards.f: Why is brand-name prescribing advised for some drugs?
cards.b: Where formulations are not interchangeable (some modified-release preparations, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, certain antiepileptics), switching products can change exposure and clinical effect.

cards.f: Name five drugs to avoid or use with great caution in pregnancy because of teratogenicity.
cards.b: Valproate, isotretinoin, warfarin, methotrexate, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and phenytoin or carbamazepine; any five.

cards.f: What core principles does shared decision making (NICE NG197) involve?
cards.b: Discussing what matters to the patient, explaining options including doing nothing, and presenting benefits and risks in understandable terms so the decision is made together.

questions.q: Which expression gives the elimination half-life of a drug obeying first-order kinetics?
questions.why: Half-life rises with volume of distribution and falls with clearance: t½ = ln2 × Vd ÷ CL, and ln2 ≈ 0.693.

questions.q: A renally cleared drug is continued on the same regimen after the patient's clearance halves; volume of distribution is unchanged. Which statement is correct?
options: Half-life doubles and the average steady-state concentration doubles
Half-life is unchanged but the steady-state concentration doubles
Half-life doubles but the steady-state concentration is unchanged
Half-life halves and the steady-state concentration doubles
questions.why: t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL, so halving CL doubles t½; average steady-state concentration equals dosing rate ÷ CL, so it also doubles, and takes twice as long to reach.

questions.q: A reversible competitive antagonist is added to an isolated tissue preparation. What happens to the agonist's log concentration–response curve?
options: Parallel shift to the right with unchanged maximum response
Parallel shift to the left with increased maximum response
Reduced maximum response with no change in EC50
questions.why: Competitive antagonism is surmountable: more agonist restores the full response, so Emax is unchanged and EC50 increases.

questions.q: Through which receptor does salbutamol produce bronchodilation?
questions.why: Salbutamol is a β2 agonist; Gs coupling raises cAMP in airway smooth muscle and causes relaxation.

questions.q: A patient has taken regular morphine for cancer pain for several months. To which effect is tolerance least likely to have developed?
questions.why: Little tolerance develops to opioid constipation or miosis, which is why laxatives are co-prescribed for as long as the opioid continues.

questions.q: Where does furosemide act?
options: Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
questions.why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb; thiazides act on the distal tubule and amiloride on ENaC.

questions.q: Under NICE NG136, which step 1 antihypertensive is preferred for a 50-year-old woman of Black African family origin who has type 2 diabetes?
questions.why: Anyone with type 2 diabetes starts on an ACE inhibitor or ARB whatever their age or family origin, and NICE suggests an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor for people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin.

questions.q: How do benzodiazepines act?
options: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening
questions.why: Benzodiazepines bind at the α/γ subunit interface of GABA-A receptors and enhance the effect of GABA by increasing opening frequency.

questions.q: A man stable on lithium is started on a new drug and develops coarse tremor and confusion within two weeks. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.why: Thiazides cause sodium loss, which increases proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium and raises its plasma level.

questions.q: Why does allopurinol interact dangerously with azathioprine?
options: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, which inactivates mercaptopurine
It induces CYP3A4, which converts azathioprine to a toxic metabolite
It blocks renal tubular secretion of azathioprine
questions.why: Xanthine oxidase is a major route of mercaptopurine inactivation; inhibiting it causes accumulation and severe myelosuppression.

questions.q: Which is an additional legal requirement for a Schedule 2 controlled drug prescription in the UK?
options: The total quantity written in both words and figures
The prescriber's GMC number written in words
A countersignature by a pharmacist before issue
The patient's NHS number written in figures and words
questions.why: Schedule 2 and 3 prescriptions must state the form, strength and total quantity in words and figures; they are valid for 28 days.

questions.q: After equal oral and intravenous doses of a drug, the areas under the plasma concentration–time curve are 24 and 40 respectively (same units). Calculate the oral bioavailability and give two reasons why it is less than 1.
markScheme: Incomplete absorption from the gut (e.g. poor solubility, efflux transporters such as P-glycoprotein, degradation in the gut lumen).
First-pass metabolism in the gut wall and/or liver before the drug reaches the systemic circulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Oral bioavailability is the ratio of the dose-normalised AUCs: F = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6, so 60% of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. It falls short of 1 because some drug is never absorbed, for example through poor solubility, breakdown in the gut lumen or efflux by P-glycoprotein. Absorbed drug then passes through the gut wall and liver via the portal vein, where first-pass metabolism removes a further fraction before it reaches the systemic circulation.

questions.q: Explain how a partial agonist can act as an antagonist, using one clinical example.
markScheme: A partial agonist has lower efficacy than a full agonist, so even at full receptor occupancy it produces a submaximal response.
In the presence of a full agonist it competes for the same receptors; occupied receptors produce less activation, so the overall response falls (net antagonism).
Valid example, e.g. buprenorphine displacing heroin or methadone at μ-receptors and precipitating withdrawal, or varenicline reducing the reward from nicotine.
questions.modelAnswer: A partial agonist binds the receptor and activates it, but its efficacy is lower than that of a full agonist, so its maximum effect is submaximal even when every receptor is occupied. If a full agonist is already present, the partial agonist competes for the same sites. Each receptor it takes over is activated less strongly, so the total response falls. Buprenorphine has high affinity but limited efficacy at μ-opioid receptors; given to someone with heroin on board, it displaces the heroin and can precipitate withdrawal.

questions.q: In an animal study the median effective concentration of a drug is 0.8 and the median toxic concentration is 2.4 (same units). Calculate the therapeutic index and explain two limitations of this measure for clinical prescribing.
markScheme: Therapeutic index = TD50 ÷ ED50 = 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 3.
Interprets: a value of 3 is narrow, meaning toxic concentrations are close to effective ones and monitoring would be needed.
Limitation: it uses median values, so ignores the slopes of the curves and the overlap between effective and toxic responses in individual patients.
Limitation: toxicity depends on which adverse effect is measured, and animal data may not transfer to humans or to individuals with altered pharmacokinetics (renal impairment, interactions).
questions.modelAnswer: TI = TD50 ÷ ED50 = 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 3. This is a narrow margin: concentrations that help most patients are only threefold below those that harm half of them, so a drug like this would need careful titration and probably drug-level monitoring. The measure has limits. It compares medians, so it ignores the slopes of the two curves; with shallow curves some patients will be harmed at concentrations that others need. It also depends on which toxic endpoint is chosen, and animal data may not predict human responses, especially in patients with renal impairment or interacting drugs.

questions.q: Predict the effects of a muscarinic antagonist such as atropine on four organ systems.
markScheme: Heart: tachycardia (block of vagal M2 tone on the SA node), with enhanced AV conduction.
Eye: mydriasis and cycloplegia (blurred near vision); can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Glands: dry mouth, reduced bronchial secretions and reduced sweating (risk of hyperthermia).
Gut and bladder: reduced motility (constipation) and urinary retention; CNS confusion or agitation at higher exposure.
questions.modelAnswer: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors throughout the parasympathetic system. In the heart, removal of vagal M2 tone causes tachycardia and faster AV conduction, which is why it is used for symptomatic bradycardia. In the eye it causes mydriasis and paralysis of accommodation, and can trigger angle-closure glaucoma. Salivary, bronchial and sweat gland secretion falls, giving a dry mouth and hot, dry skin. Gut motility and detrusor contraction are reduced, causing constipation and urinary retention, and central effects include agitation and confusion.

questions.q: Explain how suxamethonium causes neuromuscular blockade and why it carries particular risks in some patients.
markScheme: Acts as an agonist at nicotinic NM receptors, causing sustained depolarisation of the motor end-plate.
The surrounding voltage-gated Na⁺ channels become inactivated, so further action potentials cannot be generated: fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis (phase I block).
Metabolised by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase; inherited or acquired deficiency, or organophosphate exposure, causes prolonged apnoea requiring ventilation until it wears off.
Anticholinesterases do not reverse phase I block and may deepen it.

Risks hyperkalaemia, especially where extrajunctional receptors proliferate (burns, crush injury, denervation), and triggers malignant hyperthermia in RYR1-susceptible patients, treated with dantrolene.
questions.modelAnswer: Suxamethonium is a depolarising blocker: it activates nicotinic receptors at the end-plate and, because it is not broken down by acetylcholinesterase, keeps the membrane depolarised. Nearby Na⁺ channels become inactivated, so after brief fasciculations the muscle becomes flaccid. It is hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase, so patients with genetic deficiency or organophosphate exposure may remain paralysed for hours and need ventilation. Neostigmine does not reverse this block and may deepen it. Depolarisation releases potassium, which is dangerous after burns, crush injuries or denervation, where extrajunctional receptors multiply. It is also a trigger for malignant hyperthermia, treated with dantrolene.

questions.q: Explain how paracetamol overdose damages the liver and how acetylcysteine prevents this.
markScheme: Normally most paracetamol is conjugated (glucuronidation and sulfation); a small fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI.
In overdose, conjugation pathways saturate, so more NAPQI is formed.
NAPQI is detoxified by glutathione; once glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis.
Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione (as a cysteine donor) and is most effective when started early after ingestion.
questions.modelAnswer: Most paracetamol is conjugated with glucuronide or sulfate and excreted, but a small fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, a reactive metabolite that is normally mopped up by glutathione. In overdose, the conjugation pathways saturate, more drug goes down the CYP2E1 route and glutathione stores are exhausted. Free NAPQI then binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis, which is most marked in zone 3 where CYP2E1 is concentrated. Acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis and so restores detoxification; it works best when started early.

questions.q: Explain why ACE inhibitors can cause acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, and name the situation in which AKI is most likely.
markScheme: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, maintaining glomerular filtration pressure when renal perfusion is reduced.
ACE inhibition dilates the efferent arteriole, so GFR falls, most markedly in bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis in a single functioning kidney), or with dehydration, diuretics or NSAIDs.
Reduced angiotensin II lowers aldosterone secretion, reducing distal K⁺ excretion and causing hyperkalaemia.
Practical point: check creatinine and potassium before starting and after initiation or dose changes, and withhold during dehydrating illness (sick-day rules).
questions.modelAnswer: When renal perfusion pressure falls, angiotensin II maintains GFR by constricting the efferent arteriole. ACE inhibitors remove this support, so glomerular pressure and GFR drop. This matters most in bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis to a single kidney, and with dehydration, diuretics or NSAIDs. Less angiotensin II also means less aldosterone, so the collecting duct excretes less potassium and hyperkalaemia develops. Renal function and potassium should be checked before starting and after any change, and the drug paused during dehydrating illness.

questions.q: Compare serotonin syndrome with neuroleptic malignant syndrome under four headings: cause, onset, neuromuscular features and treatment.
markScheme: Cause: serotonin syndrome follows excess serotonergic activity (e.g. SSRI with MAOI, tramadol, linezolid); NMS follows dopamine D2 blockade (antipsychotics) or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs.
Onset: serotonin syndrome is rapid, within hours of a drug change; NMS develops over days.
Neuromuscular: serotonin syndrome shows clonus, hyperreflexia and tremor (often worse in the legs); NMS shows bradykinesia and lead-pipe rigidity with very high CK.
Treatment: both need the drug stopped and supportive care with cooling; serotonin syndrome may need benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine; NMS may need dantrolene or bromocriptine.
questions.modelAnswer: Serotonin syndrome is caused by too much serotonergic activity, usually after combining drugs such as an SSRI with an MAOI, tramadol or linezolid. NMS is a reaction to dopamine blockade by antipsychotics or to sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy. Serotonin syndrome comes on within hours; NMS evolves over days. Serotonin syndrome produces neuromuscular excitation, with clonus, hyperreflexia and tremor. NMS produces bradykinesia, lead-pipe rigidity and a markedly raised CK. Both need the drug stopped, cooling and supportive care. Benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine are used in serotonin syndrome; dantrolene or bromocriptine may be considered in NMS.

questions.q: A woman using a combined oral contraceptive pill is starting rifampicin. Explain the interaction and the contraceptive advice she needs.
markScheme: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer (CYP3A4 and others), increasing metabolism of ethinylestradiol and the progestogen, so contraceptive hormone levels fall and the pill may fail (Type F reaction).
Induction takes days to develop and persists for about four weeks after rifampicin is stopped.
Advise a method unaffected by enzyme inducers (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS or progestogen-only injection), or add reliable barrier methods, during treatment and for 28 days afterwards.
questions.modelAnswer: Rifampicin strongly induces hepatic enzymes, including CYP3A4, so the oestrogen and progestogen in her pill are metabolised faster. Hormone levels may drop below the level needed to suppress ovulation, and the pill can fail. The induction builds over days and takes about four weeks to wear off after rifampicin stops. She should switch to a method that enzyme inducers do not affect, such as a copper IUD, a levonorgestrel IUS or the progestogen-only injection, or use reliable additional contraception. This applies for the whole course and for 28 days afterwards.

questions.q: List four components of a complete drug history taken on hospital admission.
markScheme: Current prescribed medicines with formulation, route, frequency and indication, confirmed from at least two sources (patient, GP record, pharmacy, medicines brought in).
Over-the-counter, herbal and supplement use (e.g. St John's wort, NSAIDs) and recently stopped medicines.
Allergies and adverse reactions, specifying the drug and the nature of the reaction.
Adherence and how the patient actually takes the medicines, plus alcohol, smoking and recreational drug use.
questions.modelAnswer: A complete drug history starts with every prescribed medicine, including formulation, route, frequency and indication, checked against at least two sources such as the GP record and the patient's own supply. It should cover over-the-counter, herbal and supplement products, which patients often forget, and any recently stopped drugs. Allergies must be recorded with the specific drug and the nature of the reaction. Finally, ask how the patient actually takes their medicines, since adherence often differs from what is prescribed, and record alcohol, smoking and recreational drug use.

questions.q: A patient with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis needs analgesia and asks for something to help him sleep. Explain four prescribing concerns.
markScheme: Sedatives and opioids (e.g. benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, morphine) can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; avoid or use with great caution.
NSAIDs risk GI bleeding (varices, coagulopathy, low platelets), fluid retention and worsening ascites, and AKI or hepatorenal syndrome; avoid.
Reduced hepatic metabolism and portosystemic shunting raise bioavailability and prolong the effect of high-extraction and hepatically cleared drugs.
Hypoalbuminaemia increases the free fraction of highly bound drugs; paracetamol is often appropriate with caution, and causes of insomnia should be addressed non-pharmacologically.
questions.modelAnswer: Cirrhosis changes both pharmacokinetics and the consequences of adverse effects. Opioids and hypnotics such as benzodiazepines or Z-drugs can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy, so they are avoided or used with great caution. NSAIDs are best avoided: they increase the risk of GI bleeding from varices or coagulopathy, worsen fluid retention and ascites, and can trigger AKI or hepatorenal syndrome. Impaired hepatic metabolism and portosystemic shunting increase bioavailability and prolong the effect of many drugs, and low albumin raises the free fraction of highly bound ones. Paracetamol, used cautiously, is often the preferred analgesic, and sleep hygiene should come before drugs.

questions.q:
A new antiarrhythmic drug has a volume of distribution of 210 L and a clearance of 7 L/h in a healthy 70 kg adult. After equal oral and intravenous doses, the AUCs are 36 and 60 (same units).

(a) Calculate the elimination half-life and the oral bioavailability. (b) Estimate how long regular oral treatment will take to reach steady state and explain why a loading regimen might be used. (c) After treatment stops, how long will the plasma concentration take to fall to 25% of its steady-state value? (d) The patient later develops kidney disease that halves clearance, with Vd unchanged. Explain the effect on half-life, on time to steady state and on the steady-state concentration if the regimen is unchanged.
markScheme: F = 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6 (60%), reflecting incomplete absorption and/or first-pass metabolism.
Steady state after about 4–5 half-lives ≈ 83–104 h, i.e. roughly 3.5–4.3 days.
Loading regimen justified: for an antiarrhythmic, waiting several days for effect may be unacceptable; loading amount depends on Vd × target concentration (÷ F for oral).
Fall to 25% requires two half-lives (100% → 50% → 25%) ≈ 41.6 h.
Halving CL doubles t½ to about 41.6 h.
New steady state takes 4–5 × 41.6 h ≈ 7–9 days to reach.

Average steady-state concentration = dosing rate ÷ CL, so it doubles with an unchanged regimen, with risk of toxicity; maintenance dosing must be reduced (or interval extended) and levels/clinical effect monitored.
Notes that a large Vd (far greater than body water) implies extensive tissue binding, and that loading depends on Vd whereas maintenance depends on CL.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Half-life is t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL = 0.693 × 210 ÷ 7 = 0.693 × 30 ≈ 20.8 hours. Oral bioavailability is the ratio of AUCs after equal doses: F = 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6, so 60% of an oral dose reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. The rest is lost to incomplete absorption or first-pass metabolism. A Vd of 210 L, about five times total body water (roughly 42 L in a 70 kg adult), shows the drug is extensively bound in tissues.

(b) Steady state is reached after about four to five half-lives, roughly 83–104 hours, or about 3.5 to 4.3 days. For an antiarrhythmic that may be too long to wait, so a loading regimen can be used to reach the target concentration quickly. The loading amount is set by the volume of distribution and the target concentration, corrected for bioavailability when given orally. Maintenance dosing is then set by clearance.

(c) Each half-life halves the concentration. Falling from 100% to 25% takes two half-lives, about 41.6 hours.

(d) If clearance halves to 3.5 L/h, the half-life doubles to about 41.6 hours. The time to reach a new steady state therefore lengthens to about 7–9 days, so toxicity may build slowly and appear late. Average steady-state concentration equals dosing rate divided by clearance, so on an unchanged regimen it doubles. For a narrow-margin antiarrhythmic that could cause proarrhythmia or other toxicity. The maintenance regimen should be reduced in proportion to the fall in clearance, and the clinical effect, ECG and drug levels, where available, monitored over the following week or more. The loading requirement would not change, because Vd is unchanged.

questions.q:
Dr Okafor studies two agonists, P and Q, on an isolated smooth-muscle preparation. P has an EC50 of 10 nM and produces 100% of the maximal tissue response. Q has an EC50 of 1 nM but a maximal response of only 60%. In the presence of 10 nM of antagonist R, the concentration–response curve to P shifts to the right in parallel, with an EC50 of 40 nM and an unchanged maximum. Antagonist S reduces the maximum response to P to 50%, and washing does not restore it.

(a) Compare P and Q in terms of potency and efficacy and classify Q. (b) Predict the response when a high concentration of Q is added to tissue already maximally stimulated by P. (c) Classify R, and calculate its dissociation constant (KB) and pA2. (d) Classify S and explain its effect. (e) Give one clinical example each of the behaviours shown by Q, R and S.
markScheme: Q is more potent (lower EC50) but P has greater efficacy (higher Emax).
Q is a partial agonist.
Adding excess Q to maximal P: Q displaces P from receptors, so response falls towards Q's own maximum of about 60%.
R is a reversible competitive antagonist: parallel shift, unchanged Emax.
Dose ratio = 40 ÷ 10 = 4; Schild equation DR − 1 = [B] ÷ KB, so 3 = 10 nM ÷ KB.
S is an irreversible (or non-competitive) antagonist: it reduces Emax and the effect is not removed by washing; recovery requires new receptor synthesis.
Mentions spare receptors: at low concentrations an irreversible antagonist may first shift the curve before depressing Emax.
Clinical example of partial agonist (buprenorphine, varenicline, aripiprazole).
Clinical example of competitive antagonist (naloxone at μ-receptors, atropine at muscarinic receptors, β-blockers).
Clinical example of irreversible antagonism (phenoxybenzamine at α-receptors; aspirin on COX as an irreversible enzyme inhibitor).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Potency reflects the concentration needed for an effect, so Q (EC50 1 nM) is ten times more potent than P (EC50 10 nM). Efficacy reflects the maximal response: P produces 100% and Q only 60%. Q is therefore a partial agonist, binding with high affinity but activating the receptor less effectively.

(b) If a high concentration of Q is added to tissue already maximally stimulated by P, Q competes for the receptors and displaces P. Because each receptor Q occupies is activated less, the response falls towards Q's own maximum of about 60%. The partial agonist acts as an antagonist.

(c) A parallel rightward shift with unchanged maximum identifies R as a reversible competitive antagonist. The dose ratio is 40 ÷ 10 = 4. By the Schild equation, DR − 1 = [B] ÷ KB, so 3 = 10 nM ÷ KB, giving KB ≈ 3.3 nM. The pA2 is the negative log of the molar KB: −log10(3.3 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 8.5.

(d) S depresses the maximum response, which more agonist cannot overcome, and the effect survives washing. That fits an irreversible antagonist, probably binding covalently. The tissue can only recover by making new receptors. With spare receptors, low concentrations of such an antagonist may first shift the curve rightward before the maximum falls, because a full response needs only some of the receptors.

(e) Buprenorphine is a clinical partial agonist at μ-opioid receptors and can precipitate withdrawal in people dependent on heroin, as in (b). Naloxone is a competitive μ antagonist whose effect can be overcome by large amounts of opioid. Phenoxybenzamine irreversibly blocks α-adrenoceptors and is used before surgery for phaeochromocytoma; its effect lasts until new receptors are made.

questions.q:
Tomasz, a 45-year-old farm worker, is brought to the emergency department after spraying crops without protective equipment. He is confused, drooling and sweating heavily, with diarrhoea and urinary incontinence. His heart rate is 42/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 28/min, with widespread wheeze and copious bronchial secretions. His pupils are pinpoint, and there are fasciculations in his arms and calves with generalised weakness. His clothes smell of chemicals.

(a) What is the likely diagnosis and mechanism? (b) Classify his clinical features by receptor type. (c) Outline his immediate management, explaining the pharmacological basis of each drug used. (d) Why should suxamethonium be avoided if he needs intubation?
markScheme: Diagnosis: organophosphate (anticholinesterase) poisoning.
Mechanism: irreversible phosphorylation of acetylcholinesterase, so ACh accumulates at all cholinergic synapses; 'ageing' makes inhibition permanent.
Muscarinic features: salivation, sweating, diarrhoea, urinary incontinence, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis.

Nicotinic features: fasciculations and weakness at the neuromuscular junction (risk of respiratory failure); ganglionic stimulation may cause tachycardia or hypertension in some patients. Confusion reflects central effects.
Staff protection and decontamination: PPE, remove clothing, wash skin.
ABCDE with high-flow oxygen, suction, airway protection and ventilation if respiratory muscle weakness.
Atropine (competitive muscarinic antagonist), titrated to dry secretions, clear chest and adequate heart rate and BP; does not reverse nicotinic weakness.
An oxime such as pralidoxime may be given to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before ageing (with specialist/poisons centre advice; evidence of benefit is mixed).
Benzodiazepines for seizures or agitation; monitor for intermediate syndrome (delayed proximal and respiratory weakness).
Suxamethonium is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase, which is also inhibited, so paralysis is markedly prolonged; a non-depolarising agent is preferred.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The picture is organophosphate poisoning. Organophosphates phosphorylate the active site of acetylcholinesterase, inactivating it. Acetylcholine builds up at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. Over time the enzyme–inhibitor complex 'ages' and the inhibition becomes permanent.

(b) Muscarinic effects include salivation, sweating, diarrhoea, urinary incontinence, bronchospasm with bronchorrhoea, bradycardia and miosis. Nicotinic effects at the neuromuscular junction cause fasciculations followed by weakness, which can progress to respiratory failure. Ganglionic stimulation can sometimes cause tachycardia or hypertension instead. Confusion reflects central cholinergic excess.

(c) Staff must wear protective equipment. His clothing should be removed and his skin washed to stop further absorption. Assess with ABCDE: give high-flow oxygen, suction secretions and get early anaesthetic help, because weakness and bronchorrhoea threaten the airway and ventilation. Atropine is the key antidote. As a competitive muscarinic antagonist, it is titrated until secretions dry, the chest clears, and heart rate and blood pressure are adequate. Pupil size is not the target. Atropine does not reverse nicotinic weakness. An oxime such as pralidoxime may be given on poisons-centre advice to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before ageing, although trial evidence is mixed. Benzodiazepines treat seizures and agitation. He needs monitoring for intermediate syndrome, a delayed weakness of proximal, neck and respiratory muscles 1–4 days after exposure.

(d) Suxamethonium is normally hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase, which the organophosphate also inhibits. Paralysis could therefore last far longer than expected, and the drug adds to an already depolarised neuromuscular junction. A non-depolarising agent such as rocuronium is preferred.

questions.q:
Mrs Adeyemi, aged 71, is two days after a laparotomy and has been using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump. She was also given regular ibuprofen. Today she is difficult to rouse, with a respiratory rate of 7/min, SpO2 89% on air and pinpoint pupils; she has occasional myoclonic jerks. Her urine output has fallen, and creatinine has risen from 80 to 210 µmol/L since surgery.

(a) Explain why she has developed opioid toxicity despite controlling her own analgesia. (b) Describe her immediate management, including how and why naloxone should be used carefully. (c) What contributed to her AKI, and how should her analgesia be managed from now on?
markScheme: PCA is designed to be self-limiting (a sedated patient stops pressing), but toxicity can still occur when elimination falls.
Morphine is glucuronidated to morphine-6-glucuronide (active, μ agonist) and morphine-3-glucuronide (neuroexcitatory, linked to myoclonus); both are renally excreted and accumulate in AKI.
Immediate: stop the PCA, ABCDE, airway support, oxygen, and bag–mask ventilation if needed; call for help.
Naloxone, a competitive μ antagonist, given in small titrated increments to restore adequate breathing rather than full reversal, which would cause severe pain and sympathetic surge.
Naloxone's duration is shorter than that of the accumulated morphine metabolites, so repeat boluses or an infusion and close monitoring are needed.
AKI contributors: NSAID (loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation), perioperative hypovolaemia, possibly sepsis or nephrotoxins; stop ibuprofen, assess fluid status, review all drugs.

Ongoing analgesia: regular paracetamol, regional or local techniques if possible, and if an opioid is required, a cautious choice less dependent on renal excretion (e.g. fentanyl or alfentanil) with specialist pain/renal advice and close monitoring.
Recognise and document the ADR; report via Yellow Card where appropriate; laxative and antiemetic review.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) PCA is meant to be self-limiting: a drowsy patient stops pressing the button. That safeguard fails when the drug's elimination changes. Morphine is glucuronidated in the liver to morphine-6-glucuronide, an active μ agonist, and morphine-3-glucuronide, which has neuroexcitatory effects linked to myoclonus. Both metabolites are cleared by the kidneys. Her AKI has let them accumulate, so even modest use has led to deep sedation, respiratory depression and myoclonus.

(b) Stop the PCA and call for help. Assess with ABCDE, support the airway, give oxygen and use bag–mask ventilation if breathing is inadequate. Naloxone is a competitive μ-opioid antagonist. It should be given in small, titrated increments with the aim of restoring adequate ventilation and rousability, not full reversal. Abrupt complete reversal would cause severe postoperative pain, agitation and a catecholamine surge. Naloxone's action is shorter than that of the accumulated metabolites, so she will probably need repeat boluses or an infusion, with continuous monitoring of respiratory rate, sedation score and oxygen saturation.

(c) Her AKI probably comes from several factors. Ibuprofen removes the prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation that protects GFR when renal perfusion is threatened. Perioperative fluid losses and possible sepsis add to this. Ibuprofen should be stopped, her fluid status assessed and corrected, and all nephrotoxic or renally cleared drugs reviewed. For ongoing analgesia, regular paracetamol forms the base, plus regional or wound-infiltration techniques where available. If an opioid is still needed, use one less dependent on renal excretion, such as fentanyl or alfentanil, with acute pain team or renal advice and close monitoring. The reaction should be documented in her notes and allergy/ADR record and reported via the Yellow Card scheme.

questions.q: "Selective COX-2 inhibitors solved one problem of NSAID therapy only to create another." Critically evaluate this statement with reference to the pharmacology of cyclo-oxygenase and the key clinical trial evidence.
markScheme: Explains COX-1 (constitutive: gastric mucosal prostaglandins, platelet thromboxane A2, renal) vs COX-2 (inducible in inflammation; also constitutive in kidney, endothelium).
