Rationale for coxibs: retain anti-inflammatory/analgesic effect while sparing gastric COX-1, reducing ulcers and bleeding.
Evidence of GI benefit: VIGOR (2000) showed fewer serious upper GI events with rofecoxib than naproxen.
VIGOR also showed more myocardial infarctions with rofecoxib; APPROVe (2004) showed raised thrombotic risk vs placebo, leading to rofecoxib's worldwide withdrawal in 2004.
Mechanism of thrombotic risk: reduced endothelial prostacyclin (COX-2) with preserved platelet thromboxane A2 (COX-1) shifts balance towards thrombosis and vasoconstriction.

Nuance: the CNT Collaboration meta-analysis (Lancet, 2013) found high-dose diclofenac and ibuprofen carried vascular risk comparable to coxibs, while high-dose naproxen did not, so the 'new' problem is shared by traditional NSAIDs.
PRECISION (2016): celecoxib non-inferior to ibuprofen and naproxen for cardiovascular safety in arthritis patients at increased CV risk.
COX-2 selectivity does not spare the kidney: fluid retention, hypertension, AKI and heart failure risk persist.
Alternatives to achieve GI protection: non-selective NSAID plus PPI; topical NSAIDs; shortest duration and lowest effective exposure; risk stratification (GI and CV) guides choice.
Reaches a balanced conclusion: coxibs traded GI for CV risk in some patients, but the problem is really individual risk balance across the NSAID class.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cyclo-oxygenase converts arachidonic acid to prostanoids. COX-1 is constitutive and produces gastroprotective prostaglandins, platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2) and prostaglandins that support renal perfusion. COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation but is also constitutive in the kidney and vascular endothelium, where it generates prostacyclin (PGI2), a vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation. Traditional NSAIDs block both isoforms, so their analgesic benefit comes with peptic ulceration and bleeding.

The coxibs were designed to keep the anti-inflammatory effect while sparing gastric COX-1. VIGOR (2000) supported this: rofecoxib caused fewer serious upper GI events than naproxen. The same trial, however, recorded more myocardial infarctions with rofecoxib, and APPROVe (2004) showed raised thrombotic risk against placebo, leading to rofecoxib's withdrawal in 2004. The mechanism is plausible. Selective COX-2 inhibition suppresses endothelial PGI2 but leaves platelet TXA2 untouched, tipping the balance towards thrombosis.

The statement is only partly fair. The Coxib and traditional NSAID Trialists' meta-analysis (2013) found that high-dose diclofenac and ibuprofen carried vascular risks similar to coxibs, whereas high-dose naproxen did not. Cardiovascular hazard is therefore a feature of COX-2 inhibition across the NSAID class, not something coxibs created. PRECISION (2016) later found celecoxib non-inferior to ibuprofen and naproxen for cardiovascular safety in high-risk arthritis patients. Selectivity also gives no renal protection: fluid retention, hypertension, heart failure and AKI remain.

The GI benefit can be achieved in other ways, such as a non-selective NSAID with a PPI, or topical NSAIDs for superficial joints. In conclusion, coxibs did not so much create a new problem as expose a trade-off between GI and cardiovascular risk that runs through the whole class. Good prescribing assesses both risks in each patient and uses the lowest effective exposure for the shortest time.

questions.q:
Mr Lowe, a 76-year-old man, attends with palpitations and is found to be in atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 128/min. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes but no history of stroke, heart failure or vascular disease. He weighs 80 kg and his serum creatinine is 150 µmol/L. His medicines are ramipril, metformin and over-the-counter ibuprofen for knee pain. He asks whether daily aspirin would protect him from a stroke.

(a) Calculate his CHA2DS2-VASc score and his estimated creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault). (b) Recommend stroke prevention therapy, explaining the mechanism of your chosen drug class and why aspirin is inappropriate. (c) Outline rate control options with their mechanisms. (d) Identify the medicine-related issues that would increase his bleeding risk or affect drug choice.
markScheme: CHA2DS2-VASc: age ≥75 = 2, hypertension = 1, diabetes = 1; male sex = 0; total 4.

Recommend anticoagulation (NICE NG196 offers anticoagulation at a score of 2 or more); a DOAC is first line, e.g. apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors) or dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor).
Explains mechanism: direct inhibition of factor Xa (or thrombin) reduces thrombin generation and fibrin formation in the left atrial appendage.
Renal function must be considered when choosing and adjusting a DOAC, using CrCl per product information; dabigatran is most renally dependent.
Aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF: it is much less effective than anticoagulation and still causes bleeding.

Rate control: β-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol; β1 blockade slows AV nodal conduction) or rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem/verapamil; L-type Ca²⁺ channel block at the AV node); digoxin for sedentary patients (vagal and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase effects).
Bleeding risk assessed with ORBIT; modifiable factors addressed.
Stop ibuprofen: NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk with anticoagulants and with ramipril worsen renal function; offer topical NSAID or other knee pain management.
Metformin review given reduced renal function; check eGFR and monitor renal function; check for other interacting drugs (e.g. strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors or inducers).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) CHA2DS2-VASc: age 75 or over scores 2, hypertension 1 and diabetes 1. There is no heart failure, prior stroke, vascular disease or female sex point, so the total is 4. Cockcroft–Gault: CrCl = (140 − 76) × 80 × 1.23 ÷ 150 = 6297.6 ÷ 150 ≈ 42 mL/min, which is moderately reduced.

(b) With a score of 4, his annual stroke risk is substantial and NICE NG196 recommends offering anticoagulation. A DOAC is preferred to warfarin: no routine INR monitoring, fewer interactions and less intracranial haemorrhage. Apixaban, edoxaban and rivaroxaban directly inhibit factor Xa, while dabigatran inhibits thrombin. Both actions reduce thrombin generation and fibrin formation in the stagnant left atrial appendage. His creatinine clearance must be used to choose and adjust the drug according to its product information. Dabigatran is the most renally dependent, so it is less attractive here. Aspirin on its own is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. It is far less effective than anticoagulation and still carries a bleeding risk.

(c) A β1-selective β-blocker such as bisoprolol slows AV nodal conduction by reducing sympathetic drive. A rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) blocks L-type channels in the AV node. These two should not be combined, and the CCBs are avoided in HFrEF. Digoxin, which increases vagal tone, is an option for sedentary patients or as an add-on.

(d) Over-the-counter ibuprofen is the main problem. With an anticoagulant it greatly increases the risk of GI bleeding, and with ramipril it threatens his renal function, the 'double whammy'. It should be stopped and his knee pain managed with exercise, topical NSAID or paracetamol. Bleeding risk can be assessed with the ORBIT score. Renal function needs regular monitoring because both the DOAC and metformin depend on it, and metformin should be reviewed against his eGFR. Check for interacting drugs that strongly inhibit or induce CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein before starting.

questions.q: "In chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the drugs that save lives are those that block neurohormonal activation, not those that improve haemodynamics." Discuss, with reference to drug mechanisms and landmark trials.
markScheme: Explains pathophysiology: reduced output activates the RAAS and sympathetic nervous system; initially compensatory, these drive remodelling, fibrosis, arrhythmia and progression.
ACE inhibitors: CONSENSUS (1987) showed reduced mortality with enalapril in severe HF; mechanism includes reduced angiotensin II and aldosterone.
β-blockers: CIBIS-II (bisoprolol) and MERIT-HF (metoprolol succinate), both 1999, reduced mortality despite being negatively inotropic in the short term; need to start low and titrate.
MRAs: RALES (1999) showed spironolactone reduced mortality; aldosterone drives fibrosis and K⁺/Mg²⁺ loss.
ARNI: PARADIGM-HF (2014) showed sacubitril–valsartan superior to enalapril; neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides.

SGLT2 inhibitors: DAPA-HF (2019) and EMPEROR-Reduced (2020) reduced cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation; mechanism not purely neurohormonal (natriuresis, metabolic and other effects), which tests the proposition.
Haemodynamic drugs without survival benefit: loop diuretics relieve congestion but have no proven mortality benefit; digoxin (DIG trial, 1997) reduced hospitalisation without changing mortality.
Positive inotropes such as milrinone increased mortality (PROMISE, 1991), illustrating harm from short-term haemodynamic improvement.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate (vasodilators) showed benefit in V-HeFT and A-HeFT (2004, self-identified Black patients), a partial counterexample.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion: the statement is broadly true but oversimplified.
questions.modelAnswer:
In HFrEF, falling cardiac output activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and the sympathetic nervous system. In the short term this maintains perfusion pressure. Sustained activation, however, causes vasoconstriction, sodium retention, myocardial fibrosis, remodelling and arrhythmia, and drives the disease forward. The proposition holds that survival depends on interrupting this cycle rather than on improving the pump directly.

Most of the evidence supports it. CONSENSUS (1987) showed that enalapril reduced mortality in severe heart failure. β-blockers are the most striking case: they are negatively inotropic and can worsen symptoms at first, yet CIBIS-II and MERIT-HF (both 1999) showed large mortality reductions, probably through reduced catecholamine toxicity, heart rate and arrhythmia. RALES (1999) showed that spironolactone lowered mortality by blocking aldosterone-driven fibrosis and electrolyte loss. PARADIGM-HF (2014) found sacubitril–valsartan superior to enalapril; it adds neprilysin inhibition, raising natriuretic peptides that oppose RAAS activity.

Haemodynamic drugs tell the other side of the story. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but have no proven survival benefit. In the DIG trial (1997), digoxin reduced hospitalisation without changing mortality. Positive inotropes such as milrinone increased mortality in PROMISE (1991), despite improving haemodynamics in the short term.

The proposition is still too neat. SGLT2 inhibitors reduced cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation in DAPA-HF (2019) and EMPEROR-Reduced (2020). Their mechanism seems to involve natriuresis, osmotic diuresis and metabolic effects, not primarily neurohormonal blockade. Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate, a vasodilator combination, improved survival in V-HeFT and in self-identified Black patients in A-HeFT (2004).

In conclusion, the statement captures a central lesson: improving cardiac performance in the short term can harm, while blocking maladaptive neurohormonal activation saves lives. But it understates benefit from drugs whose actions extend beyond neurohormonal blockade. Modern therapy combines all four prognostic classes, with diuretics for symptoms.

questions.q:
Ms Greene, a 52-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, has taken lithium for 10 years with stable levels. Three weeks ago her GP started bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, and she has been taking ibuprofen for back pain. For four days she has had vomiting and diarrhoea. She now has a coarse tremor, slurred speech, an ataxic gait and confusion. Her serum lithium is 2.4 mmol/L (taken 12 hours after her last tablet), well above her usual range, and her creatinine has risen from 85 to 160 µmol/L. ECG shows sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening.

(a) Explain the factors that led to lithium toxicity. (b) Outline her management. (c) Describe the long-term monitoring and adverse effects relevant to lithium therapy.
markScheme: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is excreted almost entirely by the kidney; it is filtered and largely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule along with sodium.
Thiazide causes sodium depletion, increasing compensatory proximal reabsorption of sodium and lithium, raising levels.
NSAID reduces renal prostaglandins, lowering GFR and lithium clearance.
Vomiting and diarrhoea cause dehydration and sodium loss, further reducing clearance and causing AKI, a vicious cycle.
Features consistent with neurotoxicity (coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, confusion); risk of seizures and coma.
Management: stop lithium, bendroflumethiazide and ibuprofen; ABCDE; IV fluids (isotonic saline) to restore volume and promote excretion; monitor fluid balance, U&E, lithium levels serially, ECG.
Activated charcoal is ineffective for lithium; whole-bowel irrigation only for large modified-release overdoses (not this case).
Haemodialysis indicated for severe toxicity, particularly with renal impairment, reduced consciousness, seizures or failure to improve; discuss with poisons/renal teams.
Long term: levels regularly (taken about 12 h post-dose), renal function, thyroid function, calcium; weight and BMI.

Long-term adverse effects: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia, weight gain; teratogenicity counselling; patient education on interacting drugs and sick-day rules.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. It is freely filtered, and the proximal tubule then reabsorbs most of it alongside sodium. Anything that depletes sodium or lowers GFR raises the level. Bendroflumethiazide causes sodium loss, prompting increased proximal reabsorption of sodium and, with it, lithium. Ibuprofen inhibits the renal prostaglandins that maintain GFR, further reducing clearance. Four days of vomiting and diarrhoea then caused dehydration, more sodium loss and AKI, which retained more lithium in a vicious cycle. Her coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia and confusion show neurotoxicity, which can progress to seizures and coma.

(b) Stop lithium, the thiazide and the NSAID. Assess her with ABCDE, monitor her on a cardiac monitor and correct hypovolaemia with intravenous isotonic saline. This restores GFR and sodium delivery and so promotes lithium excretion. Monitor fluid balance, electrolytes, creatinine and serial lithium levels, because levels can rebound as lithium redistributes from tissues. Activated charcoal does not bind lithium. Seek poisons-centre and renal advice early. Haemodialysis is indicated for severe toxicity, especially with impaired renal function, reduced consciousness, seizures or failure to improve with fluids. Neurological recovery may lag behind falling blood levels. Restart lithium only after psychiatric review, and treat her hypertension with a drug that does not interact.

(c) Long-term therapy needs regular lithium levels, taken about 12 hours after the last dose, plus monitoring of renal function, thyroid function, calcium, weight and BMI. Long-term adverse effects include hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia and weight gain. Patients should know the early signs of toxicity. They should avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs and stay well hydrated, and check with a clinician or pharmacist before new medicines are started. Anyone who could become pregnant should be counselled about pregnancy planning.

questions.q:
Mr Pratt, a 68-year-old man, takes simvastatin, warfarin for atrial fibrillation, and amlodipine. His GP prescribes a week of clarithromycin for a chest infection. Five days later he presents with severe generalised muscle pain, weakness and dark brown urine. He has extensive bruising on his arms. Investigations show creatine kinase greatly raised, creatinine 240 µmol/L (baseline 90), potassium 6.1 mmol/L and INR 7.8 (target range 2–3). Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells.

(a) Explain the mechanisms of each drug interaction that has occurred. (b) Classify the adverse reactions. (c) Outline his management. (d) How could these interactions have been prevented?
markScheme: Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; simvastatin is extensively metabolised by CYP3A4, so its levels rise, causing myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (simvastatin with clarithromycin is contraindicated).
Amlodipine is a weak CYP3A4 inhibitor that also increases simvastatin exposure (additive).
Warfarin potentiation: clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of warfarin (mainly the R-enantiomer) and antibiotic effects on gut flora and acute illness can further raise the INR.
Interprets results: dipstick blood without red cells indicates myoglobinuria; AKI from myoglobin tubular toxicity; hyperkalaemia from muscle breakdown and AKI.
Classification: Type A (dose/concentration-related, predictable) pharmacokinetic interactions.

Management: stop simvastatin and clarithromycin; ABCDE; aggressive IV fluids with urine output monitoring; treat hyperkalaemia (ECG, calcium gluconate for myocardial protection, insulin–glucose, review need for renal replacement therapy).
Withhold warfarin; give vitamin K according to INR and bleeding status per local protocol; prothrombin complex concentrate if major bleeding; monitor INR.
Choose an alternative antibiotic if still needed (e.g. one without CYP3A4 inhibition, guided by local policy).
Prevention: check interactions before prescribing; choose a non-interacting antibiotic (e.g. amoxicillin or doxycycline as per guidance) or temporarily stop simvastatin; arrange early INR check.
Report via Yellow Card; document; counsel patient; review statin choice on recovery.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Clarithromycin is a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4, the main route of simvastatin metabolism. Simvastatin levels rose sharply and caused myotoxicity progressing to rhabdomyolysis; the combination is contraindicated. Amlodipine is a weak CYP3A4 inhibitor and adds to simvastatin exposure. Warfarin is a racemate. Its R-enantiomer is metabolised partly by CYP3A4, so clarithromycin raises warfarin levels. Disruption of gut flora and the acute illness can increase sensitivity further, and his INR has risen to 7.8. A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria. Myoglobin damages the renal tubules, causing AKI, and the potassium comes from both muscle breakdown and reduced excretion.

(b) These are Type A reactions: concentration-dependent, predictable from pharmacology and arising from pharmacokinetic interactions.

(c) Stop simvastatin and clarithromycin and assess him with ABCDE. Give generous intravenous fluids and monitor urine output and electrolytes closely. Treat the hyperkalaemia: do an ECG, give calcium gluconate if there are ECG changes, and give insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells. Involve the renal team early, because worsening AKI, refractory hyperkalaemia or fluid overload may need renal replacement therapy. Withhold warfarin. Give vitamin K according to the INR and bleeding status under local protocol, and use prothrombin complex concentrate if there is major bleeding. Recheck the INR daily. If an antibiotic is still needed, choose one without CYP3A4 inhibition.

(d) An interaction check at the time of prescribing would have flagged both problems. A non-interacting antibiotic could have been chosen, or simvastatin paused for the course, with an INR check within a few days. The reactions should be reported via the Yellow Card scheme and documented. On recovery, his statin should be reviewed and he should be counselled on the symptoms of myopathy.

questions.q: "Most adverse drug reactions are predictable, and therefore preventable." Critically discuss this statement.
markScheme: Defines ADR and outlines Rawlins–Thompson classification: Type A (augmented, predictable) vs Type B (bizarre), with later types C–F.

Evidence that Type A reactions predominate: Pirmohamed et al. (BMJ, 2004) found ADRs implicated in about 6.5% of admissions, mostly Type A, with common culprits including NSAIDs, diuretics, warfarin and aspirin; a large proportion were judged avoidable.
Mechanisms of predictability: known pharmacology, dose, pharmacokinetic factors (renal/hepatic impairment, age), interactions.
Preventive strategies: dose adjustment, therapeutic drug monitoring, interaction checking, deprescribing, electronic prescribing alerts, pharmacist review, patient education.

Type B reactions are less predictable, but pharmacogenomics converts some into predictable risks: HLA-B*57:01 and abacavir hypersensitivity; HLA-B*15:02 and carbamazepine SJS; TPMT/NUDT15 and thiopurine myelotoxicity; DPYD and fluoropyrimidine toxicity.
Limits: genetic tests have imperfect positive predictive value and depend on ancestry; many idiosyncratic reactions (e.g. drug-induced liver injury) lack markers.
Rare or delayed reactions only emerge after licensing (thalidomide; Type D), so post-marketing surveillance (Yellow Card, black triangle) is essential.
Predictable is not the same as preventable: some Type A effects are accepted trade-offs (chemotherapy myelosuppression, anticoagulant bleeding), so the aim is minimisation and informed consent.
System factors: prescribing errors, poor communication at transitions, polypharmacy; DoTS framework highlights susceptibility.
Balanced conclusion with justification.
questions.modelAnswer:
An adverse drug reaction is an unintended, harmful response to a medicine used normally. Rawlins and Thompson divided ADRs into Type A reactions, which are augmented, dose-related and predictable from pharmacology, and Type B reactions, which are bizarre and unrelated to the known mechanism. Later categories added chronic, delayed, end-of-use and failure reactions.

The statement is largely supported for Type A reactions, which make up most of the burden. In a prospective study of admissions in Merseyside, Pirmohamed and colleagues (2004) found ADRs implicated in about 6.5% of admissions. Most were Type A, caused by familiar drugs such as NSAIDs, diuretics, warfarin and aspirin, and many were judged avoidable. These reactions follow from known pharmacology combined with susceptibility factors such as age, renal impairment and interacting drugs. The DoTS framework sets out these factors. They can be reduced by appropriate drug selection and dosing, therapeutic drug monitoring, interaction checking, deprescribing, electronic prescribing alerts and pharmacist review.

Type B reactions are harder to prevent, but pharmacogenomics has made some of them predictable. Screening for HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir largely prevents hypersensitivity. HLA-B*15:02 testing reduces carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome in at-risk ancestries. TPMT or NUDT15 status guides thiopurine use, and DPYD testing identifies patients at risk of severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity. These tests are imperfect, however: their predictive value varies with ancestry, and many idiosyncratic reactions, such as most drug-induced liver injury, have no marker. Rare or delayed harms often emerge only after licensing, as thalidomide showed. This is why post-marketing surveillance through the Yellow Card scheme and black-triangle monitoring remains essential.

Predictable does not always mean preventable. Bleeding with anticoagulants and myelosuppression with chemotherapy are expected costs of effective treatment. Here the aim is to minimise harm and obtain informed consent, not to eliminate the risk. Many ADRs also stem from system failures, including errors at transitions of care, poor communication and polypharmacy.

In conclusion, a large share of ADRs are predictable and many are preventable, but 'most' overstates the case. Prevention depends on clinical vigilance, genomics, surveillance and safer systems.

questions.q:
Mrs Price, a 79-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, is admitted with a urinary tract infection. A junior doctor writes her drug chart from memory of her GP letter. The chart shows methotrexate prescribed once daily, folic acid, insulin with the abbreviation "U" used for units, trimethoprim for the UTI and enoxaparin for thromboprophylaxis. The allergy box reads only "penicillin". No weight or renal function is recorded, and the antibiotic has no indication or review date. Her eGFR on admission is 32 mL/min/1.73 m².

(a) Identify the prescribing errors and risks on this chart, explaining the potential harm from each. (b) Describe how each should be corrected. (c) Suggest system-level measures that reduce such errors.
markScheme: Methotrexate charted daily instead of once weekly: risk of fatal marrow suppression, mucositis and hepatotoxicity; must specify the weekly day.
Trimethoprim with methotrexate: both are antifolates, and trimethoprim reduces renal methotrexate clearance, causing pancytopenia; choose another antibiotic per local guidelines and sensitivities.
Reduced renal function (eGFR 32) increases methotrexate toxicity; methotrexate may need withholding during acute illness and specialist advice; check FBC/LFTs.
Abbreviation 'U' for units can be misread as a zero, causing tenfold insulin overdose; write 'units' in full.
Allergy entry lacks reaction details; clarify with patient/records whether true allergy or intolerance, since this affects antibiotic choice.

Enoxaparin without weight or renal assessment: LMWH accumulates in renal impairment, increasing bleeding risk; record weight, use renal adjustment or alternative per protocol, and complete VTE risk assessment.
Antibiotic without indication, course length or review date undermines stewardship.
Medicines reconciliation from at least two sources rather than memory; pharmacist review.
System measures: electronic prescribing with decision support and interaction alerts, standardised charts, education (e.g. PSA), high-risk medicine protocols, incident reporting and learning culture.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The most dangerous error is methotrexate charted once daily. For rheumatoid arthritis it is taken once weekly, and daily administration can cause fatal marrow suppression, mucositis and liver toxicity. Trimethoprim compounds this. It is also an antifolate and reduces renal excretion of methotrexate, so the combination can cause pancytopenia, made worse by her reduced renal function. Writing 'U' for insulin units risks it being read as a zero, leading to a tenfold overdose. The allergy box says only 'penicillin', so no one can tell whether she has had anaphylaxis or a minor intolerance, which affects antibiotic choice. Enoxaparin has been prescribed without a recorded weight or assessment of renal function. LMWH accumulates when renal function is reduced, increasing bleeding risk. The antibiotic has no indication or review date, which undermines stewardship.

(b) Reconcile her medicines from at least two sources, such as the GP record and the patient's own supply, ideally with a pharmacist. Correct methotrexate to the right weekly day, or withhold it during acute infection and renal impairment after rheumatology advice, and check FBC, renal and liver function. Replace trimethoprim with an antibiotic that does not interact, chosen from local guidelines and urine culture results. Rewrite insulin with 'units' in full. Document the nature of the penicillin reaction. Complete a VTE risk assessment, record her weight and prescribe thromboprophylaxis adjusted for her renal function according to local protocol. Add the indication, course length and review date to the antibiotic prescription.

(c) System measures include electronic prescribing with interaction and high-risk drug alerts and forced weekly scheduling for methotrexate. Others are standardised charts that prompt for weight, renal function and allergy reactions, pharmacist reconciliation on admission, and training such as the Prescribing Safety Assessment. A reporting culture that learns from incidents without blame also helps.

questions.q:
Mr Osei, an 88-year-old man weighing 52 kg, is admitted with urosepsis. His serum creatinine is 130 µmol/L and his reported eGFR is 46 mL/min/1.73 m². His regular medicines include metformin, apixaban for atrial fibrillation, amitriptyline for sleep, oxybutynin and furosemide. The admitting doctor plans gentamicin and regular morphine for flank pain. He has had two falls in the past month.

(a) Estimate his creatinine clearance using the Cockcroft–Gault equation and explain why it differs from his eGFR. (b) Discuss the implications for each proposed and existing medicine. (c) Using a structured approach, identify medicines that may be contributing to his falls and suggest a deprescribing plan.
markScheme: Explains discrepancy: eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m² and derived from population equations; low muscle mass and low weight in older people mean absolute clearance is overestimated; CrCl is used in many product licences.

Gentamicin: renally cleared, nephro- and ototoxic, narrow therapeutic index; avoid if suitable alternative, or use only with specialist/microbiology advice, renal-adjusted regimen and level monitoring.

Morphine: renally excreted active metabolites accumulate; risk of sedation, respiratory depression, delirium and falls; consider paracetamol and, if an opioid is needed, a cautious alternative with monitoring.
Metformin: withhold during acute illness/sepsis and AKI risk (lactic acidosis risk; sick-day rules); review against renal function.
Apixaban: check dose criteria against renal function, age and weight per product information; bleeding risk with falls, but falls alone are not usually a reason to stop anticoagulation.
Furosemide: may need withholding in sepsis with hypotension/dehydration; contributes to postural hypotension and AKI.
Falls contributors: amitriptyline (anticholinergic, sedating, postural hypotension), oxybutynin (anticholinergic, confusion), furosemide (hypovolaemia, urgency), opioids if started.
Uses a tool such as STOPP/START and anticholinergic burden scales; shared decision making with patient and family.

Deprescribing plan: taper and stop amitriptyline (sleep hygiene), stop or switch oxybutynin (e.g. mirabegron if needed, or non-drug bladder measures), review diuretic need, document and communicate with GP, monitor for withdrawal and symptom recurrence.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) CrCl = (140 − 88) × 52 × 1.23 ÷ 130 = 3325.9 ÷ 130 ≈ 26 mL/min. His eGFR of 46 is normalised to a body surface area of 1.73 m² and derived from population equations. In a small, elderly man with low muscle mass, creatinine production is low, so serum creatinine looks deceptively normal and eGFR overestimates his actual clearance. Many drug licences use Cockcroft–Gault, and his true clearance is probably close to 26 mL/min.

(b) Gentamicin is renally cleared, nephrotoxic and ototoxic, with a narrow therapeutic index. It should be avoided if a suitable alternative exists. If it is essential, use it only with microbiology advice, a renally adjusted regimen and level monitoring. Morphine's active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment and can cause sedation, delirium, respiratory depression and further falls. Start with regular paracetamol, and if an opioid is needed, use a cautious alternative with close monitoring. Metformin should be withheld during sepsis because of the risk of AKI and lactic acidosis, in line with sick-day guidance. The apixaban regimen must be checked against its renal, age and weight criteria. Falls alone are rarely a reason to stop anticoagulation, because stroke prevention usually outweighs the risk of bleeding. Furosemide may need to be withheld while he is septic and possibly hypovolaemic.

(c) A structured review using STOPP/START and an anticholinergic burden scale highlights amitriptyline, which is anticholinergic, sedating and causes postural hypotension. Oxybutynin adds anticholinergic load and confusion. Furosemide causes hypovolaemia and urinary urgency, which leads to hurried trips to the toilet. A newly started opioid would add to all of these. The deprescribing plan should be agreed with Mr Osei and his family. Taper and stop amitriptyline and offer sleep hygiene measures. Stop oxybutynin and use bladder training, or mirabegron if drug treatment is still needed. Review whether furosemide is still indicated, and check lying and standing blood pressure. Document the changes, tell the GP and arrange monitoring for withdrawal effects or returning symptoms.
